## The pub argument

Sunday 2 March 2025, Kavanagh's in Glasnevin (the Gravediggers), with my brother Ciarán, who is a structural engineer and a cheerful hard determinist. His line, after the second pint: "Your neurons fired, you ordered the Guinness, the ordering was never up to you." Mine: then neither is your argument, so why should I be persuaded by it? He said that was a cheap shot. It was. These are the notes I wrote on the 46A home so I can do better next time.

## Hard determinism

Every event, including every decision, is fixed by prior events and the laws of nature. If so, nobody could have done otherwise, and if nobody could have done otherwise, nobody is morally responsible. Ciarán accepts the conclusion and says we should still lock people up for the same reasons we fence off a cliff. I find that honest and chilling.

## Libet, and what it actually showed

Benjamin Libet, 1983. Subjects flexed a wrist whenever they felt like it and noted the clock position when they first felt the urge (the "W time"). The readiness potential in the motor cortex started about 350 ms before W time. Headline: the brain decides before you do.

Problems:
- The task was a meaningless flick, not a choice between options that matter.
- Reporting the clock position is itself unreliable by 50 ms or more.
- Schurger, Sitt and Dehaene (*PNAS*, 2012) argue the readiness potential is mostly accumulated background noise crossing a threshold, not a hidden decision.
- Libet himself kept a "veto": about 200 ms in which you could still stop. Free won't, he called it.

So I told Ciarán: interesting neuroscience, weak metaphysics.

## Compatibilism

Freedom is not the absence of causes but acting from your own reasons without coercion. Harry Frankfurt, "Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility", *Journal of Philosophy* 66 (1969): the scientist Black who would intervene if Jones were about to choose differently, but never needs to. Jones couldn't have done otherwise and is still responsible. That case changed my mind about twenty years ago and still does the work for me.

Daniel Dennett, *Elbow Room* (1984), and *Freedom Evolves* (2003). Dennett's line: the kinds of freedom worth wanting are compatible with determinism.

## The consequence argument

Peter van Inwagen, *An Essay on Free Will* (1983), p. 56. If determinism is true, our acts are the consequences of the laws of nature and events in the remote past. But it is not up to us what went on before we were born, and it is not up to us what the laws are. So the consequences are not up to us. The strongest argument on Ciarán's side, and he's never heard of it. I'm not telling him.

## Strawson's basic argument

Galen Strawson: to be truly responsible for what you do you'd have to be responsible for how you are, which would mean having chosen how you are, which needs an earlier self that chose that, and so on. Can't be done. Neat, a bit too neat.

## Sapolsky

Robert Sapolsky, *Determined* (2023). €24.99 in Hodges Figgis, 12 Jan 2025. p. 46: "we are nothing more or less than the sum of that which we could not control". Readable, generous, and philosophically quite thin; he doesn't really engage with Frankfurt.

## Where I am now

- Compatibilist on responsibility, agnostic on the physics.
- What we do with blame matters more than the metaphysics: Ciarán and I agree on prison reform for opposite reasons.
- The Stoics were compatibilists before the word existed: Chrysippus' cylinder, rolled by a push but rolling by its own shape. Ties into [[Stoicism daily practice]].
- Sartre would call all of this bad faith; see [[Existentialism reading list]].

Brought this up in TY after the [[Trolley problem]] lesson, when Darragh asked whether the brake-cutter "could help it".
